title: Cadmium removal from acidic wastewater using coconut–rice husk‐activated carbon: Adsorption behavior and fluorescence‐assisted monitoring
content:
Abstract

Activated carbon derived from a coconut husk–rice husk composite was investigated for Cd2+ removal using a laser-induced fluorescence (LIF) technique. The material was prepared through carbonization followed by chemical activation. It was subsequently characterized using Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) analysis. The adsorbent exhibited a porous structure with oxygen-containing surface functional groups and a BET surface area of approximately 196 m2g−1. Adsorption experiments were conducted under acidic conditions (pH 1–4) with initial Cd2+ concentrations of 25–75 mg L−1 and adsorbent dosages of 0.2–1.2 g. Rapid Cd2+ uptake was observed, and selected samples were validated using ICP-OES to confirm fluorescence measurements. The highest experimental adsorption capacity was 22.5 mg g−1 at an initial concentration of 75 mg L−1. Adsorption kinetics followed the pseudo-second-order model (R 2 >0.98), while equilibrium data were best described by the Freundlich isotherm (R 2 ≥0.99, n = 1.7–2.2, KF = 9.9–19.0). The Langmuir model predicted a theoretical monolayer capacity of 31.76 mg g−1. The results are relevant to acidic industrial effluents such as electroplating and battery wastewater.
